cards.question: Describe a catalyst through its pathway, activation energy and fate overall. [3]
cards.answer: It provides an alternative reaction pathway [1] with lower activation energy [1] and is regenerated overall [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Homogenous and heterogeneous catalysts including enzymes

cards.question: Explain why a catalyst can appear in an intermediate step but not in the net reaction equation. [2]
cards.answer: It participates temporarily in the steps [1]; because it is regenerated later, it cancels when the steps are added [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Homogenous and heterogeneous catalysts including enzymes

cards.question: Describe homogeneous and heterogeneous catalysts and the basis of their distinction. [3]
cards.answer: A homogeneous catalyst shares the reactants’ phase [1]; a heterogeneous catalyst is in another phase [1]; classification concerns phase rather than rate or biological origin [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Homogenous and heterogeneous catalysts including enzymes

cards.question: Explain how a solid catalyst can act repeatedly with gaseous reactants at its surface. [2]
cards.answer: Reactants associate with surface sites and react through that route [1]; products leave, making the sites available again [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Homogenous and heterogeneous catalysts including enzymes

cards.question: Describe a catalyst’s effect on the Boltzmann distribution and energy threshold at fixed temperature. [3]
cards.answer: The distribution curve stays the same [1]; the alternative pathway has a lower Ea [1]; a larger fraction of the existing particles has sufficient energy [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Homogenous and heterogeneous catalysts including enzymes

cards.question: Explain why a catalyst raises rate without increasing the average kinetic energy at fixed temperature. [2]
cards.answer: It provides a lower-Ea pathway [1]; because more of the unchanged energy distribution lies above that threshold, more encounters can react [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Homogenous and heterogeneous catalysts including enzymes

cards.question: Draw one labelled Boltzmann distribution at fixed temperature, with separate catalysed and uncatalysed Ea thresholds. Show which threshold gives more particles with sufficient energy. [2]
cards.answer:
A correct sketch has energy horizontally, particle population per energy interval vertically, and one rising then falling long-tailed curve [1]; the catalysed Ea lies left of the uncatalysed Ea, with a greater area beyond the lower threshold [1].

One normalized energy distribution at fixed relative temperature 2.5. The catalysed threshold is at energy 4 and uncatalysed at 7. The extra region between thresholds represents additional particles energetic enough for the lower-barrier route.
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Homogenous and heterogeneous catalysts including enzymes

cards.question: State what an enzyme is. [1]
cards.answer: A biological catalyst [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Homogenous and heterogeneous catalysts including enzymes

cards.question: Suggest why an enzyme converts substrate S but not molecule T in comparable tests at the same suitable pH and temperature. [1]
cards.answer: Its active-site features interact suitably with S but not T [1], giving substrate specificity.
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Homogenous and heterogeneous catalysts including enzymes

cards.question: Describe how temperature, damaging heat and pH can affect a protein enzyme’s activity. [3]
cards.answer: Moderate warming can raise rate through particle-energy effects [1]; sufficiently high heat can disrupt active-site structure and lower activity [1]; unsuitable pH can alter active-site interactions or structure [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Homogenous and heterogeneous catalysts including enzymes

cards.question: Explain why a protein enzyme can show low activity after damaging heat even when reactant collisions would otherwise be faster. [2]
cards.answer: The heat can denature the protein and alter its active site [1]; because substrate interaction/catalysis is impaired, the catalyst loses activity despite faster particle motion [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Homogenous and heterogeneous catalysts including enzymes

cards.question: Describe first ionisation energy, including amount basis, starting particles and final particles. [3]
cards.answer: Energy needed to remove one electron from each atom in one mole [1] of gaseous atoms [1], forming one mole of gaseous 1+ ions [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Periodicity of physical properties of elements in Period 3

cards.question: Explain why the first ionisation equation X(g) → X+(g) + e− has a positive energy requirement. [2]
cards.answer: The electron is attracted to the positive nucleus [1]; energy must be supplied to overcome that attraction and separate it [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Periodicity of physical properties of elements in Period 3

cards.question: Describe three factors relevant to the attraction holding an outer electron before first ionisation. [3]
cards.answer: Nuclear charge [1], distance of the electron from the nucleus [1], and shielding by inner electrons [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Periodicity of physical properties of elements in Period 3

cards.question: Explain why increased nuclear charge alone does not prove a greater first ionisation energy when comparing atoms down a group. [2]
cards.answer: Additional shells increase distance and inner-electron shielding [1]; these can reduce effective attraction despite the extra protons [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Periodicity of physical properties of elements in Period 3

cards.question: Describe the general Period 3 trends in atomic radius, the isoelectronic Na+/Mg2+/Al3+ radii, and electronegativity from sodium to chlorine. [3]
cards.answer: Atomic radius generally decreases [1]; Na+ > Mg2+ > Al3+ in radius [1]; electronegativity generally increases from sodium to chlorine [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Periodicity of physical properties of elements in Period 3

cards.question: Explain why Al3+ is smaller than Na+, given that both ions have ten electrons. [2]
cards.answer: Al3+ has greater nuclear charge [1]; its nucleus attracts the same number of electrons more strongly, contracting the ion [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Periodicity of physical properties of elements in Period 3

cards.question: Describe the general first-ionisation-energy trend across Period 3 and its main nuclear explanation. [3]
cards.answer: It generally increases [1]; nuclear charge rises [1], while comparable inner shielding and falling radius strengthen attraction to the removed electron [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Periodicity of physical properties of elements in Period 3

cards.question: Explain why the outer electron of a Period 3 atom near the right-hand end is generally harder to remove than sodium’s outer electron. [2]
cards.answer: Nuclear charge is larger without a new main shell of inner shielding [1]; the effective attraction is greater and radius smaller, requiring more removal energy [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Periodicity of physical properties of elements in Period 3

cards.question: Describe the structures and ordinary conduction of aluminium, silicon and molecular sulphur. [3]
cards.answer: Aluminium is metallic and conducts through delocalised electrons [1]; silicon is giant covalent and semiconducting [1]; sulphur contains S8 molecules and is a poor conductor [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Periodicity of physical properties of elements in Period 3

cards.question: Explain why silicon has a much higher melting point than molecular chlorine. [2]
cards.answer: Silicon melting disrupts an extended strong covalent network [1]; chlorine melting overcomes much weaker intermolecular attractions between Cl2 molecules [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Periodicity of physical properties of elements in Period 3

cards.question: Describe how comparable atomic/ionic radii and electronegativity generally change down Groups 2 and 17. [3]
cards.answer: Atomic radii increase [1]; comparable ionic radii increase [1]; electronegativity generally decreases [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Trends in physical properties of elements down a group

cards.question: Explain why the chloride ion is larger than the fluoride ion. [2]
cards.answer: Cl− has an additional occupied shell [1]; the outer electrons are farther from the nucleus and more shielded, so the ion is larger [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Trends in physical properties of elements down a group

cards.question: Describe the general first-ionisation trend down Groups 2 and 17 and the two shell-related causes. [3]
cards.answer: First ionisation energy generally decreases [1]; outer electrons are farther from the nucleus [1] and more shielded by inner electrons [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Trends in physical properties of elements down a group

cards.question: Explain why a lower Group 2 atom generally loses its first electron more easily despite having more protons. [2]
cards.answer: Extra shells increase distance and shielding [1]; the resulting weaker effective attraction outweighs the increased nuclear charge in this group comparison [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Trends in physical properties of elements down a group

cards.question: Describe the products of magnesium reacting with oxygen, cold water and steam. [3]
cards.answer: Oxygen gives MgO [1]; cold water reacts slowly to form Mg(OH)2 and H2 [1]; steam gives MgO and H2 [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Periodicity of chemical properties of the elements in Period 3

cards.question: Write the balanced equation for phosphorus P4 forming phosphorus(V) oxide in excess oxygen. Include state symbols. [2]
cards.answer: P4(s) + 5O2(g) → P4O10(s). Correct product/states [1]; balance [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Periodicity of chemical properties of the elements in Period 3

cards.question: Write the balanced equation for sodium with cold liquid water. Include state symbols. [2]
cards.answer: 2Na(s) + 2H2O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H2(g). Correct products/states [1]; balance [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Periodicity of chemical properties of the elements in Period 3

cards.question: Explain why a magnesium–water equation should state whether water is cold liquid or steam. [2]
cards.answer: Cold water reacts slowly and gives magnesium hydroxide [1]; steam reacts more readily with heated magnesium and gives magnesium oxide, so the stated medium affects both rate and product [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Periodicity of chemical properties of the elements in Period 3

cards.question: Describe the maximum oxidation numbers in the specified highest oxides from sodium through sulphur, their direction of change and the valence-electron connection. [3]
cards.answer: They are +1, +2, +3, +4, +5 and +6 [1], increasing across the stated series [1] as formal maximum participation follows increasing valence-electron count [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Periodicity of chemical properties of the elements in Period 3

cards.question: Explain why Al2Cl6 assigns aluminium +3 rather than +6. [2]
cards.answer: Six chlorines contribute −6 overall [1]; two aluminium atoms share the balancing +6 total, giving each +3 [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Periodicity of chemical properties of the elements in Period 3

cards.question: Explain the error in a claimed maximum-oxide oxidation-number trend that rises to aluminium and then falls towards sulphur. Use P4O10 and SO3 as a discriminating test. [2]
cards.answer: It incorrectly predicts falling values for the non-metals [1]; charge balance gives phosphorus +5 and sulphur +6, continuing the increase in the specified highest oxides [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Periodicity of chemical properties of the elements in Period 3

cards.question: Describe the water reaction of Na2O, Al2O3 and P4O10 in the ordinary comparison. [3]
cards.answer: Na2O forms alkaline sodium hydroxide [1]; Al2O3 does not react appreciably [1]; P4O10 forms phosphoric(V) acid [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Periodicity of chemical properties of the elements in Period 3

cards.question: Write the balanced equation for P4O10 reacting with water to form phosphoric(V) acid. Include state symbols. [2]
cards.answer: P4O10(s) + 6H2O(l) → 4H3PO4(aq). Correct species/states [1]; balance [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Periodicity of chemical properties of the elements in Period 3

cards.question: Explain why lack of reaction between SiO2 and ordinary water does not show that SiO2 is a basic oxide. [2]
cards.answer: Acid/base classification is not determined by water solubility alone [1]; SiO2 reacts with strong alkali under suitable heating, supporting acidic-oxide behaviour [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Periodicity of chemical properties of the elements in Period 3

cards.question: Describe basic, acidic and amphoteric oxide behaviour in reactions with acids and sodium hydroxide. [3]
cards.answer: A basic oxide reacts with acid [1]; an acidic oxide reacts with sodium hydroxide under suitable settings [1]; an amphoteric oxide can react with both [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Periodicity of chemical properties of the elements in Period 3

cards.question: Explain why aluminium oxide is described as amphoteric. [2]
cards.answer: It reacts with acid to give aqueous aluminium-containing salt species and water [1], and with sodium hydroxide to give an aluminate product under suitable settings [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Periodicity of chemical properties of the elements in Period 3

cards.question: Describe the differences when NaCl, AlCl3 and SiCl4 are added to excess water. [3]
cards.answer: NaCl dissolves to an approximately neutral solution [1]; hydrated aluminium ions produce an acidic solution by hydrolysis [1]; SiCl4 hydrolyses to silica and HCl [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Periodicity of chemical properties of the elements in Period 3

cards.question: Write the simplified balanced hydrolysis equation for SiCl4 in excess water, giving SiO2 and HCl. Include state symbols. [2]
cards.answer: SiCl4(l) + 2H2O(l) → SiO2(s) + 4HCl(aq). Correct products/states [1]; atom balance [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Periodicity of chemical properties of the elements in Period 3

cards.question: Explain why an acidic conducting solution after SiCl4 hydrolysis does not prove the original pure liquid was ionic. [2]
cards.answer: SiCl4 reacts with water to form new substances including acid [1]; ions in those products carry solution current, so that observation is not direct evidence of original liquid ions [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Periodicity of chemical properties of the elements in Period 3

cards.question: State the general change in bonding descriptions of the selected oxides and chlorides as Period 3 electronegativity rises. [1]
cards.answer: Descriptions change from predominantly ionic towards more covalent character [1], with structure- and state-specific qualifications.
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Periodicity of chemical properties of the elements in Period 3

cards.question: Determine which structure better fits an oxide that is very high-melting and does not conduct as a solid or ordinary liquid: a simple molecular solid or a giant covalent network. [1]
cards.answer: A giant covalent network [1]; high melting point and lack of mobile charge fit that description better.
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Periodicity of chemical properties of the elements in Period 3

cards.question: State the conduction observation that supports mobile ions appearing on melting a compound. [1]
cards.answer: It does not conduct as a solid but conducts when molten [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Periodicity of chemical properties of the elements in Period 3

cards.question: Explain why high melting point alone cannot distinguish an ionic oxide from a giant covalent oxide. [2]
cards.answer: Both contain strong interactions throughout extended structures [1]; additional evidence such as molten conduction is needed to identify mobile ions rather than a covalent network [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Periodicity of chemical properties of the elements in Period 3

cards.question: State the common ion charge predicted for a typical Group 2 metal. [1]
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Chemical periodicity of other elements

cards.question: Suggest the atomic-radius change for a Group 17 element below chlorine compared with chlorine. [1]
cards.answer: A larger radius [1], because additional shells increase distance and shielding.
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Chemical periodicity of other elements

cards.question: State why several independent properties are preferable to one broad observation when identifying an unknown Period 3 element. [1]
cards.answer: A broad property can fit several candidates, while additional independent clues discriminate between them [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Chemical periodicity of other elements

cards.question: Determine the Period 3 element that conducts as a metal, forms a common 2+ ion and gives a basic oxide. [1]
cards.answer: Magnesium [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Chemical periodicity of other elements

cards.question: State whether Group 2 melting points follow a strictly decreasing pattern down the group. [1]
cards.answer: No [1]; the pattern is irregular, including calcium above magnesium.
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Similarities and trends in the properties of the Group 2 metals

cards.question: Explain why increasing atomic radius alone cannot justify a strictly decreasing sequence of Group 2 melting points. [2]
cards.answer: Radius affects metallic attraction [1], but the result also depends on solid structure, so departures in measured melting points must be retained [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Similarities and trends in the properties of the Group 2 metals

cards.question: Describe the products of magnesium with oxygen, calcium with cold water, and calcium with dilute hydrochloric acid. [3]
cards.answer: MgO with oxygen [1]; Ca(OH)2 and H2 with cold water [1]; CaCl2 and H2 with dilute HCl [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Similarities and trends in the properties of the Group 2 metals

cards.question: Write the balanced equation for calcium reacting with dilute hydrochloric acid. Include state symbols. [2]
cards.answer: Ca(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl2(aq) + H2(g). Correct species/states [1]; balance [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Similarities and trends in the properties of the Group 2 metals

cards.question: Write the balanced equation for magnesium reacting with steam. Include state symbols. [2]
cards.answer: Mg(s) + H2O(g) → MgO(s) + H2(g). Correct products and steam state [1]; balance [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Similarities and trends in the properties of the Group 2 metals

cards.question: Explain why calcium generally reacts with cold water more readily than magnesium, considering outer electrons. [2]
cards.answer: Calcium’s outer electrons are farther from the nucleus and more shielded [1]; their weaker effective attraction makes electron loss easier [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Similarities and trends in the properties of the Group 2 metals

cards.question: State the gas formed when a Group 2 carbonate reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid. [1]
cards.answer: Carbon dioxide [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Similarities and trends in the properties of the Group 2 metals

cards.question: Suggest why sparingly soluble magnesium hydroxide can still react with dilute hydrochloric acid. [1]
cards.answer: Acid consumes its basic hydroxide, allowing further solid to react; low water solubility does not prevent neutralisation [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Similarities and trends in the properties of the Group 2 metals

cards.question: State the products of sufficient heating of a Group 2 nitrate in the school decomposition pattern. [1]
cards.answer: The metal oxide, nitrogen dioxide and oxygen [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Similarities and trends in the properties of the Group 2 metals

cards.question: Suggest the gas evolved when pure calcium carbonate is heated sufficiently to form calcium oxide. [1]
cards.answer: Carbon dioxide [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Similarities and trends in the properties of the Group 2 metals

cards.question: State the general thermal-stability trend for Group 2 carbonates down the group. [1]
cards.answer: Thermal stability increases [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Similarities and trends in the properties of the Group 2 metals

cards.question: Determine whether a carbonate of a Group 2 metal below calcium is generally expected to decompose more or less readily under comparable heating. [1]
cards.answer: Less readily [1], because thermal stability generally increases down the group.
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Similarities and trends in the properties of the Group 2 metals

cards.question: State the opposite down-group solubility trends for Group 2 hydroxides and sulphates. [1]
cards.answer: Hydroxides generally become more soluble; sulphates generally become less soluble [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Similarities and trends in the properties of the Group 2 metals

cards.question: Explain the predicted change when moving from calcium to barium in hydroxide and sulphate solubility under comparable aqueous settings. [2]
cards.answer: Barium hydroxide is expected to be more soluble [1], whereas barium sulphate is less soluble, so the two compound families must be treated separately [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Similarities and trends in the properties of the Group 2 metals

cards.question: State the name and composition of the product formed when lime reacts with water. [1]
cards.answer: Slaked lime, calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)2 [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Some uses of Group 2 compounds

cards.question: Suggest why a lime–water mixture becomes hot while forming slaked lime. [1]
cards.answer: Slaking is exothermic and transfers heat to the mixture [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Some uses of Group 2 compounds

cards.question: Describe the chemical roles of limestone in acidic soil, limestone in cement manufacture, and slaked lime in lime mortar. [3]
cards.answer: Limestone neutralises soil acidity [1]; it supplies calcium-containing raw material for cement compounds [1]; slaked lime can react with air’s CO2 to harden as carbonate in lime mortar [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Some uses of Group 2 compounds

cards.question: Explain why powdered limestone can help treat an acidic soil, including the purpose of powdering. [2]
cards.answer: Its carbonate consumes H+ and can raise pH [1]; powdering increases exposed surface and speeds acid contact/reaction [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Some uses of Group 2 compounds

cards.question: Describe the syllabus criterion for a transition element in terms of table block, ions and d occupancy. [3]
cards.answer: It is a d-block element [1] forming one or more ions [1] with an incomplete d subshell [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Characteristics of typical transition elements

cards.question: Explain why copper meets the syllabus transition-element criterion despite its atom having 3d10. [2]
cards.answer: The criterion includes the ions it forms [1]; Cu2+ is 3d9, so it has an incomplete d subshell [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Characteristics of typical transition elements

cards.question: State the electronic configuration of Fe2+ using an argon core. [1]
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Characteristics of typical transition elements

cards.question: Explain why Fe2+ has [Ar]3d6 rather than [Ar]3d4 4s2. [2]
cards.answer: The 4s electrons are removed before 3d when forming these ions [1]; removing iron’s two 4s electrons leaves the six 3d electrons [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Characteristics of typical transition elements

cards.question: State three characteristic chemical properties of transition elements. [1]
cards.answer: Variable oxidation states, catalytic activity and formation of coloured compounds [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Characteristics of typical transition elements

cards.question: Suggest the characteristic transition-element property illustrated by Fe2+ and Fe3+ forming in different compounds. [1]
cards.answer: Variable oxidation states [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Characteristics of typical transition elements

cards.question: Describe typical transition metals compared with calcium in density, melting point and conduction. [3]
cards.answer: They generally have higher densities [1] and higher melting points [1], while both show metallic electrical conduction [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Characteristics of typical transition elements

cards.question: Contrast iron with calcium in typical density and melting point, while recognising their shared metallic character. [2]
cards.answer: Both are metals, but iron is denser [1] and has a higher melting point than calcium [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Characteristics of typical transition elements

cards.question: State the three metal-ore examples used for Namibia in this syllabus section. [1]
cards.answer: Copper, manganese and uranium [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Extraction of transition elements from their ores

cards.question: Suggest why including uranium among Namibian extraction examples does not make uranium a first-row d-block transition metal. [1]
cards.answer: The examples concern extraction; uranium is an actinide rather than a first-row d-block element [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Extraction of transition elements from their ores

cards.question: State the redox role of carbon when it removes oxygen from a suitable metal oxide. [1]
cards.answer: It is the reducing agent [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Extraction of transition elements from their ores

cards.question: Suggest why a carbon-reduction equation alone does not establish that the collected metal is pure. [1]
cards.answer: Ore and processing impurities may enter the product, so refining can still be needed [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Extraction of transition elements from their ores

cards.question: State what ferromanganese is in the specified mixed-oxide reduction route. [1]
cards.answer: An iron–manganese alloy that can contain carbon and other impurities [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Extraction of transition elements from their ores

cards.question: Suggest why a mixture of iron oxide and manganese oxide can give ferromanganese rather than pure manganese when reduced with carbon. [1]
cards.answer: Both metal-bearing feeds contribute reduced metals to the common alloy product [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Extraction of transition elements from their ores

cards.question: State the function of sulphuric acid in a suitable metal-ore leaching route. [1]
cards.answer: It transfers suitable metal-bearing material into soluble species for later recovery [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Extraction of transition elements from their ores

cards.question: Suggest why CuO reacting with sulphuric acid to give CuSO4 solution has not yet produced copper metal. [1]
cards.answer: Copper remains in the +2 state in solution; a later reduction to Cu(0) is needed [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Extraction of transition elements from their ores

cards.question: State the reducing agent in the syllabus’s prepared-compound route to uranium metal. [1]
cards.answer: Magnesium [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Extraction of transition elements from their ores

cards.question: Suggest the cathode electron-transfer step for recovering copper metal from a prepared Cu2+ leach solution. [1]
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Extraction of transition elements from their ores

cards.question: State one gaseous pollutant associated with roasting sulphide ores. [1]
cards.answer: Sulphur dioxide [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Extraction of transition elements from their ores

cards.question: Explain why neutral pH alone does not demonstrate that treated leach waste is free of toxic metals. [2]
cards.answer: pH indicates acidity rather than metal concentration [1]; metal species can remain dissolved or be transferred into waste solids, so they need separate monitoring [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Extraction of transition elements from their ores

cards.question: State what makes metal ores finite resources. [1]
cards.answer: The usable geological deposits are limited and are not replaced on human extraction timescales [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Extraction of transition elements from their ores

cards.question: Explain why recycling metal can reduce fresh-ore demand while still producing waste. [2]
cards.answer: Recovered metal replaces some new extraction [1], but sorting, contamination and recovery losses leave residues requiring handling [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Extraction of transition elements from their ores

cards.question: State the colour of iodine vapour. [1]
cards.answer: Violet/purple [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Physical properties of the group 17 elements

cards.question: Suggest why iodine can appear brown in an aqueous layer but violet in a suitable non-polar organic layer. [1]
cards.answer: Its solution colour depends on solvent/species context; those are the expected aqueous and non-polar appearances [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Physical properties of the group 17 elements

cards.question: State the physical states of chlorine, bromine and iodine at ordinary room temperature and pressure. [1]
cards.answer: Chlorine gas, bromine liquid, iodine solid [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Physical properties of the group 17 elements

cards.question: Explain why the room-temperature state changes from chlorine gas to iodine solid. [2]
cards.answer: The larger molecular electron clouds give stronger dispersion attractions down the sequence [1], raising phase-transition temperatures so iodine remains solid at room temperature [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Physical properties of the group 17 elements

cards.question: State the relative volatility order for chlorine, bromine and iodine at comparable settings. [1]
cards.answer: Chlorine > bromine > iodine [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Physical properties of the group 17 elements

cards.question: Determine whether a rise in boiling point from Cl2 to I2 indicates weaker or stronger intermolecular attractions. [1]
cards.answer: Stronger attractions [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)Physical properties of the group 17 elements

cards.question: State the oxidising-strength order of chlorine, bromine and iodine. [1]
cards.answer: Chlorine > bromine > iodine [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)The chemical properties of the elements and their hydrides

cards.question: Suggest the elemental halogen produced when chlorine reacts with aqueous bromide. [1]
cards.answer: Bromine [1], because chlorine oxidises Br−.
cards.lesson_title: (L1)The chemical properties of the elements and their hydrides

cards.question: Describe how hydrogen reacts with chlorine, bromine and iodine in the school comparison. [3]
cards.answer: Chlorine can react rapidly/explosively when initiated by light [1]; bromine requires heating [1]; iodine reacts reversibly at elevated temperature to give HI [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)The chemical properties of the elements and their hydrides

cards.question: Write the balanced gas-phase equation for hydrogen with chlorine forming hydrogen chloride. [2]
cards.answer: H2(g) + Cl2(g) → 2HCl(g). Correct species/states [1]; balance [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)The chemical properties of the elements and their hydrides

cards.question: Explain why a weaker halogen–halogen bond alone does not prove a more vigorous reaction with hydrogen. [2]
cards.answer: The energy account also includes breaking H–H and forming two H–X bonds [1]; the pathway barrier and the complete energy balance, rather than one bond, determine the comparison [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)The chemical properties of the elements and their hydrides

cards.question: Describe the thermal-stability order HCl, HBr and HI and the down-group bond change explaining it. [3]
cards.answer: HCl > HBr > HI [1]; H–X bonds become longer [1] and weaker, making thermal decomposition easier [1].
cards.lesson_title: (L1)The chemical properties of the elements and their hydrides
